content: Plasmodium vivax (P. vivax) is a significant focus in the global effort to eliminate malaria, particularly in regions where it coexists with Plasmodium falciparum. This is further complicated by the presence of asymptomatic carriers of P. vivax, as well as the fact that treatment protocols for P. vivax and Plasmodium ovale differ from those used for other malaria species. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are essential tools for distinguishing P. vivax from other malaria species, aiding in both appropriate treatment and elimination efforts. These RDTs function by detecting P. vivax parasitemia through the identification of P. vivax-specific lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) antigens. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of RDTs in detecting P. vivax malaria among individuals in endemic areas who present to outpatient healthcare facilities with symptoms suggestive of malaria. Additionally, the study aimed to identify which types and brands of commercially available RDTs are most effective in detecting P. vivax malaria. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to July 30, 2019, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others. Studies were included if they compared RDTs to a reference standard, such as microscopy or polymerase chain reaction (PCR), using blood samples from symptomatic patients in P. vivax-endemic areas. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers using a pre-piloted data extraction form. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Studies were grouped by the commercial brand of the RDT, and meta-analyses were conducted when appropriate. The diagnostic accuracy of the RDTs was evaluated based on antibody affinity and avidity, and all analyses were stratified by the type of reference standard used. A bivariate model was employed to estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 10 studies that evaluated the accuracy of six different RDT brands: CareStart Malaria Pf/Pv Combo test, Falcivax Device Rapid test, Immuno-Rapid Malaria Pf/Pv test, SD Bioline Malaria Ag Pf/Pv test, OnSite Pf/Pv test, and Test Malaria Pf/Pv rapid test. One study directly compared the accuracy of two RDT brands. Of the 10 studies, six used microscopy as the reference standard, one used PCR, two used both microscopy and PCR separately, and one used microscopy corrected by PCR. The studies were conducted in Ethiopia (4 studies), India (2 studies), and one study each in Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia, and Sudan. The studies often lacked detailed reporting on patient selection methods, leading to an unclear risk of bias in nine studies. All studies were judged to have unclear applicability concerns. In the domain of the index test, most studies were at low risk of bias, but nine studies were judged to have unclear applicability concerns. Reporting on lot testing, RDT storage conditions, and background parasitemia density—a critical factor influencing diagnostic accuracy—was generally poor. Only half of the studies were judged to have a low risk of bias in the reference standard domain. Many studies did not clarify whether the reference standard could accurately classify the target condition or whether investigators were blinded to the RDT results when interpreting the reference standard. However, all 10 studies were judged to have a low risk of bias in the flow and timing domain. Only two RDT brands were evaluated by more than one study. Four studies assessed the CareStart Malaria Pf/Pv Combo test against microscopy, while two studies evaluated the Falcivax Device Rapid test against microscopy. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for the CareStart Malaria Pf/Pv Combo test were 99% (95% CI: 94% to 100%) and 99% (95% CI: 99% to 100%), respectively, based on moderate-certainty evidence. For a prevalence of 20%, approximately 206 individuals would test positive using the CareStart Malaria Pf/Pv Combo test, with eight false positives and two false negatives. The remaining 794 individuals would test negative. In contrast, the pooled sensitivity and specificity for the Falcivax Device Rapid test were 77% (95% CI: 53% to 91%) and 99% (95% CI: 98% to 100%), respectively, based on lowto moderate-certainty evidence. For a prevalence of 20%, approximately 162 individuals would test positive using the Falcivax Device Rapid test, with eight false positives and 46 false negatives. The remaining 838 individuals would test negative. In conclusion, the CareStart Malaria Pf/Pv Combo test demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity compared to microscopy for detecting P. vivax in outpatient healthcare settings in endemic regions, with moderate-certainty evidence. However, the review was limited to 10 studies, and only two of the six RDT brands included in the review were evaluated in sufficient detail to estimate their diagnostic accuracy. Further high-quality studies conducted in endemic field settings are necessary to assess and compare the accuracy of RDTs designed to detect P. vivax.
